1:
Samuel's age is left without a figure, and the estimates run wide. Gill reports the common Jewish notion that he lived only fifty-two years, and adds that others put him at sixty while Abarbinel allowed more than seventy. Clarke and Wesley both settle on about sixty. Ellicott works it out from the history instead: barely thirty when the ark was taken, nearly fifty by the victory at Eben-ezer, then a stretch long enough for the Philistines to recover the southern districts, which brings him to the seventy a famous Hebrew commentator proposed and he judges likely correct. Henry will not go past sixty but accounts for the early decay another way: Samuel was a man betimes, full of cares when he was a child, and the fruits that are first ripe keep the worst. Wesley follows him closely here, down to the judge who thinks to shake himself as at other times and finds himself mistaken, age having cut his hair.

What office the sons held is agreed on by three of the voices. Clarke denies they were judges in the proper sense at all, Samuel being the last judge in Israel and judging it to the day of his death. Wesley puts it as a rule, that the supreme judgeship was held by one man only and that one of God's choosing, so the sons determined matters as deputies with appeal reserved to their father. Henry has them assistants first and then deputies stationed at Beer-sheba, remote from Ramah, and guesses that the southern districts had petitioned to have them there rather than travel far with their causes. Ellicott finds the appointment natural in a father whose circuit was growing burdensome, and notes from Josephus that only one son sat at Beer-sheba while the other judged in the north. Their names carry the atmosphere of their father's house, Joel meaning that Jehovah is God and Abiah that Jehovah is a father.

Clarke takes the iniquity apart into three charges. They turned aside after lucre; they took bribes, the Hebrew word meaning the gifts that blind a judge's eyes; and they perverted judgment, selling it to the highest bidder, so that the rich man had his cause and the poor lost his right. His note then runs off into English legal history before Magna Charta. Henry stays with the money. Lucre is the mammon of unrighteousness, as he notes the Chaldee reads it, and the love of it is pernicious in anyone but especially in a judge; deciding causes, the sons had an eye on the bribe rather than the law and asked who bid highest instead of who had right. He presses that their father had taken none, and that public justice, once perverted, does a people the greatest wrong. Keil and Delitzsch set the same three faults against the express commands in Exodus and Deuteronomy.

On how the corruption arose the two closest voices separate. Henry's rule is that many who did well in meanness and subjection have been spoiled by preferment, and that the sons discovered themselves only once they were settled out of their father's sight. Wesley reverses the order of cause: opportunity and temptation did not create the corruption but disclosed what had been in them all along and hidden from Samuel. Ellicott draws the parallel the chapter invites, that the ills which ruined Eli's house through his children now threatened Samuel's, and marks the difference in how the two men met it, the prophet-judge being himself the chief agent in setting up the king who displaced his sons. He alone follows them past their disgrace, holding that the punishment corrected them, since the family reappears in honour at David's court in Heman the grandson, chief of the singers. Henry's closing digest adds a circumstance the exposition left out, an Ammonite invasion under Nahash already threatening and sharpening the grievance.
4:
The body that came to Ramah is identified before anything else. Gill makes the elders the heads of the tribes and the fathers of the houses and families, the principal men by age and authority. Ellicott treats them as a standing institution rather than an occasion, a popular assembly traceable at every period and meeting even under the Egyptian bondage, its members qualified by birth or office. Henry marks the manner of the approach: by common consent, not riotously or in tumult, but with the respect due to Samuel's character, coming to him at his own house. The proposal itself he calls new and surprising, never till now publicly debated; Abimelech had been little better than a titular king, and his fall may once have made the title odious in Israel as Tarquin's did among the Romans, though by now the odium had worn off.

Ellicott sets out the two circumstances they built on: Samuel's age, with his consequent inability to lead them in the frontier wars; and the degeneracy of the sons placed in trust by their father and expecting to succeed him. Gill and Henry both refuse the first plea. Age was no reproach and not theirs to throw at him, Gill answers, since experience had made him fitter even if he could no longer ride his circuits. Henry turns it round further: if the years made him less able to sit long on the bench they made him wiser, and he had grown old in their service, so that casting him off for it was unkind, ungrateful and unjust. The second plea he grants, but not as their real motive, since Samuel had not indulged his sons as Eli did, stood ready to receive complaints, and on proof of bribery would have taken their commissions away; another project lay behind the petition.

Whether the request was itself unlawful is where the reading divides hardest. Keil and Delitzsch find the wording so close to the law of the king in Deuteronomy, down to the phrase about all the nations, that the allusion cannot be missed, and conclude that the elders asked no more than what God had foretold through Moses as a thing to come and had made provision for in advance. Henry allows only that it was well they did not set up a king by force but begged it of God's prophet; the proposal was still evil, since God meant to give them a king after his own heart when Samuel was dead, and they would anticipate his counsel. Keil and Delitzsch add that express quotation of the book of the law is not otherwise met with until the writings of the captivity.

On what the elders actually wanted the voices converge. Clarke is blunt that the surrounding nations had kings to serve as generals in battle, leaving a theocracy that had owned no king but God. Wesley holds that their desires outran their reasons, which reached no further than removing the two corrupt deputies and finding other help for Samuel's age; and he presses the remedy's defect, that a king's sons were as likely to be corrupt and, being heirs rather than appointees, not so easily removed. Against the plea of likeness he sets the separation God had made and the immediate care no other nation enjoyed. Henry puts the preference in terms of appearance: a prophet in a mantle looked mean to men who judged by the outside, where a king in a purple robe with guards and officers of state would look great; they did not ask for one wise and good, only for one who would make a figure. Ellicott alone reads the plea as a compliment, since to urge their judge's own infirmity and his children's unworthiness took confidence that he would do right against his own interest, and the event justified it.
6:
What displeased the old judge is settled by elimination. Gill rules out both personal provocations, the taunt about his age and the sight of his sons' walk, and points to the demand that follows. Clarke names the offence directly, that the petition amounted to a formal renunciation of the divine government. Wesley finds three things in it: God dishonoured by the distrust, the ambition and itch after change behind the request, and the misery Samuel foresaw for the people. Ellicott adds the personal wound, that men who owed him everything wanted a different ruler. On what he prayed for, the two shortest notes part company. Clarke has him asking only to know God's mind in so weighty a business; Wesley has him asking first for pardon of the people's sin, then for direction and help.

Ellicott holds both halves of the question at once. The elders were perfectly justified in the resolution their petition contained, because the directions for an earthly king are clear and explicit and Moses had looked forward to the change when he framed the law, fixing no date but contemplating no distant one. Yet for a man like Samuel it was bitter, and the bitterness was not personal pique. It removed Israel from the solitary platform which among all nations they alone had been allowed to occupy, and proved what Moses had predicted, that such a government did not suit them and they must come down to the level of ordinary peoples. What the hero patriot gave up for ever was the splendid ideal of a people ruled directly by the Eternal King.

The answer came, Gill says, in a vision or dream and by an articulate voice; Ellicott also judges it a vision. Clarke reads it as the transfer of a government always held by their God into the hands of a mortal, and draws the hard inference that God grants in displeasure what he withholds in mercy. Wesley puts it as punishment, the desire granted in anger, the contumely falling chiefly on God and on the immediate government that was this people's honour and safety, if they had had hearts to prize it. Gill treats the appeal to the exodus as establishing that nothing new had happened, but one continued series of ingratitude against God and the servants he employed. Wesley reduces the same verse to a word of consolation, that Samuel fared no worse than his master. Ellicott goes furthest, expanding the sentences into a speech of tenderness to an old true servant and calling the transaction sad, a deliberate lowering of the ideal once formed for the chosen people, with the veil lifted for a moment on what he ventures to call the Creator's sorrowful regret.

The order to protest is read three ways. Keil and Delitzsch work from the idiom, rejecting both the rendering that makes it an earnest warning and the one that makes it a solemn expounding; the construction means to bear witness against a person, to point out his wrong, and the clause that follows tells how, by proclaiming the king's manner. Clarke takes the manner as what a king would and might require after the fashion in which kings then ruled, all of them absolute and despotic, and borrows Puffendorf's summary of the demands to come, so the people might understand what they asked and consider whether to persist. He then turns on Grotius for inferring what a king may claim anywhere by virtue of his office: this was Saul's manner, and Saul was no king of God's choosing but given in wrath and taken away in displeasure, so no ruler claiming divine right may arrogate it, the manner of God's chosen king being set out elsewhere in the law. Wesley keeps a purpose the others let go, that the protest still hoped to prevent the sin and the misery.
10:
Gill fixes the sense of the word rendered manner before anything is listed: not the course a king ought to take but the course he will take, and not of one king or the first only but of kings in general, commonly inclined to arbitrary power. He supports it from Aristotle, who set an absolute kingdom against theocracy as the state in which a king does all things according to his will, and held that whoever would have reason preside would have God and the laws rule, while whoever would have a man reign brings in a man's appetite. Henry draws the same line as a rule for living: the law of God and the manner of men differ widely, the first the measure of what we owe in every relation of life, the second of what we may expect from others. Keil and Delitzsch record only that Samuel reported everything God had said and then proclaimed the king's right; Gill adds that he was ordered to set out the inconveniences and evils that would follow.

Ellicott reads the speech as a question rather than a reproach. Samuel does not blame the desire; he asks quietly whether they are in earnest and have weighed the constitutional change, whether they will exchange a republic for a despotism under a sovereign who, like the Pharaohs, would of course govern after his own will. He then sketches the change. There would be a gorgeous court of the kind some of them had seen on the Nile or the Euphrates, and everything choicest in Israel would be summoned to it; the pastoral life and the dwelling under their own vines would give way to a city life whose vices would draw their children off; and war would come on a scale they had never imagined.

On the conscription of the sons the philology carries the weight. Keil and Delitzsch make them retainers at court, set upon his chariots and saddle-horses and running before his carriage, and refuse to level the singular suffix into a plural as Thenius proposed on the authority of the Greek and the old versions, since the vehicle is not a war-chariot but the king's carriage of state, and the second word denotes a saddle-horse rather than its rider. Captains over thousands and fifties they take as the greatest and least of the officers named for the whole army, the verb of taking still governing the ploughing, reaping and weapon-making that follow. Ellicott glosses the old verb for ploughing, kin to the Anglo-Saxon and the Latin. Gill will not let the commissions pass as advancement: posts of honour cease to be desirable when they are not matters of choice and hang on a prince's arbitrary will. Wesley is harder, reading the taking as done injuriously and by violence, for the king's fancy and glory rather than any necessity of the kingdom, and the setting to work at his pleasure and on his own terms when the men's own fields wanted all their time.

The daughters draw more agreement. Gill takes the confectionaries for women who dealt in spices and mixed them into forms agreeable to the taste, remarks that the trade belonged to men in his own country but to women in that place, and notes the versions that make them sellers of ointments. Ellicott prefers perfumers outright, makers of the scents of which easterners are inordinately fond, and Keil and Delitzsch render it the same way, adding cooks and bakers for the court. Wesley weighs this loss differently: more grievous to the parents and more dangerous to the daughters themselves, given the tenderness of that sex and how open they lay to injury. Henry's digest leaves the catalogue aside and ends where the king's manner tends, that those who submit to the government of the world and the flesh are told plainly what hard masters they are.
14:
Whether the king could take the land itself or only what it yielded is argued from the same episode to opposite conclusions. Gill restricts the threat to the increase, the corn and wine and oil of the fields, vineyards and oliveyards, on the ground that kings neither might nor did take freeholds away by absolute authority: had that been in Ahab's power he would have taken Naboth's vineyard outright, and Jezebel would not have needed her method of getting it for him. Wesley reads the same history the other way, that fields were taken by fraud or force exactly as Ahab took Naboth's, and that the king would seize the possessions themselves and not merely the fruits, in order to give them to his servants. Keil and Delitzsch stand with Wesley: the best fields, vineyards and olive-gardens would be taken away and given to his servants, with the produce tithed for his courtiers besides.

At the mention of the goodliest young men the two grammatical voices converge on a conjecture. Keil and Delitzsch find the word striking and altogether unsuitable where it stands between the slaves and the asses, and judge it an ancient copyist's error for your oxen, the reading behind the Greek; on that supposition servants and maids answer to oxen and asses as pairs, and the young men are already comprehended among the sons listed earlier. Ellicott reaches the same result by the same two arguments, noting that the Greek reads best oxen and that only one letter of similar sound need change, and treats it as beyond doubt the original. Where they part is the word rendered officers. Keil and Delitzsch allow the literal eunuch but take it in the wider sense of royal chamberlains; Wesley keeps the literal force and makes a further charge of it, that the king would make eunuchs of his own people against the command of God and advance into his court and favour the very men God would have cast out of the congregation.

On the exactions the notes are mostly supplementary. Gill takes the tenth of the seed as falling on the grain once grown and ripe, and extends the tenth of the sheep to the herds as well, which he says Kimchi counts included. Wesley presses the novelty rather than the extent: over and above the several tenths God had reserved for his own service, the king would impose another whenever he pleased. Both read the pressing of the household as arbitrary. Gill has the menservants and maidservants taken into the royal family for the king's use if he wants them or likes them better than those he has; Wesley has them taken by constraint and without sufficient recompense.

The summary sentence is where Ellicott puts the weight. Being the king's servants gathers up everything before it: the elders must make up their minds, electing a king, to the loss of all political and social freedom. Wesley says it more bluntly, that they would be used like slaves and stripped of the liberty they enjoyed. Ellicott then follows the forecast into the history. The yoke was felt even under Solomon, and the discontent it left broke the people into two nations at his death; the northern tribes then abandoned the ark and temple for a rival and half-idolatrous worship, and under men like Omri and Ahab no prayers availed, one wicked dynasty following another until Israel was carried away captive. Gill makes the unanswered cry a matter of their own doing, since the distress was of their own bringing, and Wesley makes it reciprocal, God not hearing them then because they would not hear his counsel now. Against the critics who date the passage from the later monarchy, Keil and Delitzsch hold the picture drawn from heathen despotism and presupposing nothing later, and Ellicott borrows the same verdict from the commentary he cites.
19:
That the warning failed is agreed; how deliberately it failed is not. Gill has the people refusing the advice to want no king and to be content with the government they had, and refusing it in full view of every inconvenience set before them. Keil and Delitzsch judge that Samuel had put the dangers of a monarchy so alarmingly that the elders ought to have been brought to reflection and to have given up their demand, and instead they simply repeated it. Clarke makes the obstinacy complete: they would have the king and his manner with him, solemn warning and all. Ellicott alone gives the refusal a procedure. The prophet-judge's words were evidently considered and debated with care in a formal assembly, and it was a majority that in the end held to the terms of the original request, which makes the outcome a decision rather than a clamour.

On the motive of likeness two of the voices reach for the same word. Gill calls it stupidity that they would have a king as the nations had one even though those nations were slaves under theirs, when their greatest honour and glory and happiness lay precisely in being unlike other peoples, in religion and laws and liberties and in their form of government, God being their King in a sense in which he was no other nation's. Wesley exclaims at the same stupidity and settles on the same ground, that the Lord was their immediate king and lawgiver, and that this above their other privileges was the thing they were throwing away. Ellicott finds the terms of the request strangely painful rather than stupid. They forgot, or chose to ignore, the solitary place of pre-eminence God had given them, which they had failed to understand in the past as well; and the haste to climb down from the pedestal he had set them on looked to a man like Samuel an inexplicable foolishness.

What they wanted the king to do is read off the three clauses. Clarke takes the first as a rejection of Samuel himself, the second as a demand that the king be in every respect their head and governor, and the third as making him general of their armies; Keil and Delitzsch render the last as conducting their battles. Wesley turns the military clause against them by pointing back one chapter. Could they have asked a battle better fought than the last, which went by Samuel's prayers and God's thunder, and were they so fond of trying the chance of war at the same uncertainty as everyone else? He then answers from the event, that their first king fell in battle, as did one of the last and best of the line; the text as it stands here names that later king wrongly.
21:
The rehearsing is described four ways, and the differences are in the where and the why rather than the what. Gill keeps it indoors and silent: Samuel heard the people out patiently and without interruption, took notice of what they said and laid it up, then gave them no answer at all but carried it to the Lord. Clarke places the act at the altar, where in secret devotion he laid the whole business before God. Ellicott has the seer leave the council chamber for some quiet spot, probably the sanctuary he had set up in his own Ramah of the Watchers, and pour out his heart there. Wesley supplies the motive instead of the place, the private repetition serving at once for his own vindication and comfort and as the ground of his prayer for direction and assistance.

How the answer came Gill now leaves open, an audible voice or else an impulse on the mind, where earlier in the chapter he had spoken of a vision and an articulate voice. Ellicott counts it the third time the same expression had been used, and draws the inference that God had let his servant remonstrate while knowing throughout what the end would be, answering at the last in the self-same words he had used at the first. On the dismissal the voices fill out what the sentence leaves unsaid. Keil and Delitzsch supply the unspoken condition, that the elders were sent home until he should call them again to appoint the king they wanted. Clarke notes that they had waited with Samuel all this while and were told and dismissed only when he had his final answer, and Wesley has them sent back to their several occasions until they should hear more. Ellicott reads the form of words as evidence that they were a representative body drawn from the chief centres of the land.

Clarke sets out the whole affair in numbered propositions, and the first of them are weighty. God did not change the government of Israel; the people changed it. He permitted the king without approving him. He withheld from them the choice of the man, ordering it by a lot he himself disposed. He never resigned the supreme government, remaining King in Israel while the so-called king was only his deputy; and the proof Clarke offers is that no king of Judah ever attempted to be supreme, since none made new laws or altered the old, which he treats as a standing confession that God was the supreme Legislator. From the sixth proposition onward the note turns into constitutional argument, distinguishing absolute monarchy, which he calls always an evil and contrary to every civil and religious right, from kingly government properly understood, and then praising the mixed British constitution of king, nobles and people at length, with a closing complaint about the weight of taxes. Ellicott ends on the elders rather than the institution: they had listened respectfully, deliberated, firmly repeated their request, watched their judge go alone into the presence of God, and then dispersed quietly to their cities, loving and trusting the man they were ready to depose and waiting for him to give them the sign.
